draft:
When software turns the work schedule into a live feed, a shift can move, shrink, or disappear after a worker has arranged the rest of the day around it (its start time, length, and location). The sales pitch is efficiency. The practical effect is control—the power to claim a worker's time without paying for all of it. Unpredictability isn't only an inconvenience; it changes who gets to make plans and who must wait.

A schedule is a promise about time. When an employer posts one and then keeps rewriting it, the promise runs in only one direction. Management may revise demand whenever sales dip or orders rise, while the worker must preserve empty space around several possible shifts (an “availability window”). That reserve of unpaid time is valuable. It prevents a second job, complicates classes, and pushes care arrangements onto family members. The software doesn't merely record uncertainty; it distributes uncertainty downward—from the institution to the individual.

Consider what happens when a message arrives at noon changing an evening shift (the hours previously posted). Can a worker decline without losing future hours, falling in a manager's ranking, or being labeled unreliable? If you cannot safely say no, the notification is not a request. It is an instruction delivered through an interface. The screen may look neutral, but the consequence is physical: the worker rushes for transport, wakes a caregiver, cancels an appointment, or goes without wages.

That asymmetry disciplines workers even when no shift actually changes. A person who expects a late alteration stays close to the phone and avoids commitments (the person is effectively on standby). The employer receives flexibility; the worker absorbs the cost. A missed alert may mean missed income, and a cancelled shift may leave rent or groceries uncovered. The system won't call that coercion. It will call it optimization, a word that makes the burden sound like a settings menu.

Employers do face real changes in demand, and some scheduling flexibility can protect jobs. But flexibility does not have to mean permanent readiness from workers. The question is who bears the cost of uncertainty. A company can spread variation across staffing levels, overtime, and reserves (a weekly planning problem). An hourly worker often has fewer buffers. When every surprise is passed to the person with the least bargaining power, they're being made to finance the employer's flexibility—but without the premium that flexibility should command.

Software deepens this imbalance because rules can hide inside automated systems (the ranking logic, penalty settings, and notice thresholds). A supervisor once had to speak the demand aloud. Now an alert can make a unilateral change feel inevitable. That isn't neutrality. It is management by default—one side configures the options, and the other side lives with them. Workers may also struggle to tell whether a change came from a manager, a forecast, or a penalty rule. Ambiguity makes challenge harder.

Organizing begins by making that hidden system legible. Workers can keep records of posted schedules, later changes, lost hours, and disciplinary messages (the evidence needed to show a pattern). They can bargain for minimum notice, extra pay for late changes, compensation for cancelled shifts, and a genuine right to refuse. A rule without enforcement will not rebalance power. Complaints need a clear route, retaliation needs a consequence, and workers need access to the records the software creates. Otherwise the right exists only in a policy manual.

The public-interest standard should be simple: software shouldn't let an employer purchase flexibility with someone else's uncompensated time. Employers must provide stable schedules, vendors must expose the rules that alter them (the right to an explanation), and lawmakers must attach pay and enforceable refusal rights to short-notice changes. We should treat predictable time as part of wages and conditions, because control over hours is control over life. Our demand is not perfect forecasting. It is shared risk, clear notice, and worker consent.
